title: Kidney-Cleared Drugs: Lithium, Aminoglycosides and Methotrexate
summary: Learn why lithium, aminoglycosides and high-dose methotrexate depend on the kidney, when to draw lithium and how EXTRIP grades its levels, what a high gentamicin trough means, why aminoglycoside ear damage is the feared toxicity, and how urine alkalinisation and leucovorin protect against methotrexate.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 24 Hits 13 (lithium renal handling, 12-hour sampling, toxicity tiers, creatinine and TSH monitoring), 14 (methotrexate precipitation in acidic urine, alkalinisation, leucovorin rescue), 16 (traditional gentamicin trough below 2 µg/mL; high trough means accumulation) and 17 (aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity and often-irreversible ototoxicity). Checked against Decker 2015 (EXTRIP lithium; read via a page-fetch tool), Liu 2022, Erden 2013, Sheikh 2022, Gitlin 2016, Howard 2016, Bielack 2024, Moore 2025 and the US gentamicin prescribing information (DailyMed). Qualified against sources: EXTRIP labels 1.5–2.5 / 2.5–3.5 / >3.5 mEq/L as mild / moderate / severe and calls them only a guide, and its dialysis criteria are >4.0 with impaired kidney function, >5.0, or severe symptoms at any level (register flag rv-lithium-tiers-extrip); leucovorin typically starts 24–36 h in the European consensus and the end-point is <0.05–0.1 µmol/L, protocol-dependent (rv-mtx-leucovorin-window); the <2 µg/mL trough is the US label figure for conventional dosing, while current guidance favours once-daily dosing with AUC monitoring and troughs below 1 mg/L (rv-gentamicin-trough-current-practice). Not taught: Number Vault lithium ranges, lithium half-life, leucovorin doses, glucarpidase dosing, aminoglycoside peak/MIC targets.

objectives: Explain why lithium, aminoglycosides and methotrexate depend on kidney function, including lithium’s renal handling and methotrexate’s insolubility in acidic urine.
State when to draw a lithium level, the EXTRIP steady-state severity guide, the extracorporeal treatment criteria and the long-term creatinine and thyroid monitoring.

Interpret a high gentamicin trough, contrast reversible nephrotoxicity with generally irreversible ototoxicity, and outline urine alkalinisation and level-guided leucovorin rescue for high-dose methotrexate.

scenes.title: Three kidneys, three numbers
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three inpatients whose drugs leave the body through the kidneys. (1) A patient on long-term lithium, drowsy and hard to rouse, serum lithium 2.8 mEq/L drawn 12 hours after the last dose. (2) A patient on gentamicin every 8 hours with a trough of 3.2 µg/mL. (3) A patient about to start high-dose methotrexate whose urine pH is 5.5. Question token: “What does each number mean, and what happens next?”

cues.text: Three patients, three drugs, one exit: the kidney. A drowsy patient on lithium has a level of two point eight, drawn twelve hours after the last dose.
A patient on gentamicin every eight hours has a trough of three point two. And a patient about to start high-dose methotrexate has a urine pH of five point five.
What does each number mean, and what should happen next?

props.label: What does each number mean? What next?

scenes.title: One exit: the kidney
scenes.altText: Schematic nephron with three drug cards. Lithium: a small cation with properties similar to sodium; not protein bound (0%), not metabolised, freely filtered and excreted entirely in urine; about 80% of the filtered load is reabsorbed (about 60% proximal tubule, 20% thick ascending limb). Aminoglycosides: mainly excreted by the kidneys, so falling kidney function means accumulation. Methotrexate: more than 90% eliminated by the kidneys; it and its metabolites are poorly soluble in acidic urine and can crystallise in the tubules (crystals form in urine below pH 5.5 at high tubular concentrations), causing acute kidney injury.

cues.text: Lithium behaves like sodium. It is not bound to protein and is not metabolised; it is filtered freely and leaves only in the urine. About eighty percent of what is filtered is reabsorbed, mostly in the proximal tubule.
Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin are also cleared mainly by the kidneys, so when kidney function falls, the drug accumulates.
More than ninety percent of methotrexate is eliminated by the kidneys. Methotrexate is poorly soluble in acidic urine, and at high doses it can crystallise in the tubules and injure the kidney.
So for all three drugs, kidney function and the timing of the blood sample decide what a level means.

scenes.title: Lithium: when to draw and how high is too high
scenes.altText: Lithium timing card: peak plasma concentrations come within hours of an oral dose, so routine levels are drawn about 12 hours after the last dose. Severity card (EXTRIP 2015, steady-state levels, “only a guide”): mild toxicity 1.5–2.5 mEq/L, moderate 2.5–3.5, severe above 3.5. Extracorporeal treatment card (EXTRIP): recommended if kidney function is impaired and lithium is above 4.0 mEq/L, or with decreased consciousness, seizures or life-threatening dysrhythmias whatever the level; suggested above 5.0; after dialysis, lithium can rebound as it redistributes, so repeat levels. Monitoring card (Gitlin 2016): serum creatinine and eGFR every 6–12 months; thyroid tests (TSH) before starting and during treatment.

cues.text: Lithium peaks within a few hours of an oral dose, so a level drawn then reads high. Routine levels are drawn about twelve hours after the last dose.

The EXTRIP workgroup gives a rough guide for steady-state levels: one point five to two point five is mild toxicity, two point five to three point five moderate, and above three point five severe. The authors stress these are only a guide.

Dialysis is recommended when kidney function is impaired and lithium is above four, or with reduced consciousness, seizures or dangerous arrhythmias at any level, and suggested above five. Lithium can rebound after dialysis, so levels are repeated.
Long-term treatment needs regular serum creatinine and eGFR, every six to twelve months, and thyroid tests such as TSH, because lithium can injure the kidney and cause hypothyroidism.

scenes.title: Gentamicin troughs and methotrexate rescue
scenes.altText: Gentamicin card (US prescribing information): for conventional every-8-hour dosing, the trough is drawn just before the next dose and dosage is adjusted so troughs above 2 µg/mL (and prolonged peaks above 12 µg/mL) are avoided; a rising trough means accumulation; in kidney impairment one method is to lengthen the interval between usual doses. Toxicity card: nephrotoxicity is generally reversible; vestibular and auditory toxicity are generally irreversible. Current practice note (Moore 2025): once-daily dosing with AUC monitoring in adults; trough below 1 mg/L for multiple-daily synergy dosing. Methotrexate card: hydration with bicarbonate to urine pH of at least 7 before infusing; leucovorin rescue typically starts 24–36 hours after methotrexate, with doses set by serial levels from 24 hours, continued until methotrexate is below about 0.05–0.1 µmol/L; after glucarpidase, immunoassays cross-react with the metabolite DAMPA, so chromatography (HPLC) is more reliable. Hook answers: (1) decreased consciousness → extracorporeal treatment recommended whatever the level; (2) trough too high → accumulation, lengthen the interval, check kidney function; (3) do not start until urine pH ≥ 7.

cues.text: For traditional gentamicin every eight hours, the trough is drawn just before the next dose, and the label says to adjust dosing so troughs above two are avoided. A high trough means the drug is accumulating; one fix is to lengthen the interval, not to push the dose.
Kidney injury from aminoglycosides is generally reversible, but damage to hearing and balance is generally permanent. Many centres now give once-daily doses and monitor the area under the curve.

For high-dose methotrexate, the urine is alkalinised to a pH of at least seven before infusion. Leucovorin rescue typically starts twenty-four to thirty-six hours after methotrexate, guided by serial levels, until methotrexate falls below about zero point zero five to zero point one micromolar. After glucarpidase, immunoassays read falsely high, so chromatography is preferred.

Back to the hook. The drowsy lithium patient meets dialysis criteria whatever the level. The gentamicin trough is too high, so lengthen the interval and check the kidneys. And methotrexate waits until the urine pH reaches seven.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A lithium level drawn 2 hours after the dose shows toxicity” (✓ levels peak within hours; draw about 12 hours after the last dose); “A high gentamicin trough means the dose should go up” (✓ a high trough means accumulation; lengthen the interval and check kidney function); “Aminoglycoside toxicity always reverses when the drug stops” (✓ kidney injury is generally reversible, but hearing and balance damage is generally permanent).

cues.text: Trap one: a lithium level drawn two hours after the dose proves toxicity. No: lithium peaks within hours. Draw about twelve hours after the last dose.
Trap two: a high gentamicin trough means you should raise the dose. No: a high trough means accumulation. Lengthen the interval and check the kidneys.
Trap three: aminoglycoside damage always reverses when the drug stops. No: the kidney usually recovers, but hearing and balance damage is generally permanent.

scenes.title: One exit, three gatekeepers
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “ONE EXIT, THREE GATEKEEPERS.” Lithium is the salt twin: the kidney treats it like sodium, so draw it at 12 hours. Gentamicin is the trough guard: a high trough means the exit is jammed, so space the doses. Methotrexate is the acid crystal: keep the urine alkaline (pH 7) and send leucovorin to rescue. Tokens: Li = 12 h · gentamicin = trough · MTX = pH 7 + leucovorin. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: one exit, three gatekeepers. Lithium is sodium’s twin, so draw it at twelve hours. Gentamicin’s trough tells you the exit is jammed, so space the doses. Methotrexate forms crystals in acid, so keep the urine at pH seven and send leucovorin.

Where it breaks: lithium levels are only a guide, and symptoms such as reduced consciousness can call for dialysis at any level; aminoglycoside ear damage can occur even with careful dosing in genetically susceptible patients; and many centres now monitor gentamicin by area under the curve, with lower trough targets.

explanation.what: Plain language: these three drugs leave the body almost only through the kidney, so if the kidney slows or the urine is wrong, the drug builds up and hurts the patient. The lab tells the team how much is in the blood, but only if the sample is drawn at the right time. Scientific terms: renal clearance, tubular reabsorption, protein binding, steady state, trough concentration, accumulation, extended interval, area under the concentration–time curve (AUC), nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity (vestibular and auditory), crystal nephropathy, urine alkalinisation, leucovorin rescue, glucarpidase, DAMPA, extracorporeal treatment (EXTRIP).
explanation.why: Lithium is filtered and largely reabsorbed like sodium, so anything that changes salt and water balance changes its level; aminoglycosides accumulate when clearance falls; methotrexate and its metabolites are poorly soluble in acidic urine and can crystallise in the tubules, and its elimination is followed by serial levels.
explanation.measure: Lithium: draw about 12 h after the last dose; EXTRIP steady-state guide 1.5–2.5 mild, 2.5–3.5 moderate, >3.5 mEq/L severe; extracorporeal treatment recommended if kidney function is impaired and >4.0, or with decreased consciousness, seizures or life-threatening dysrhythmias at any level, suggested if >5.0; creatinine/eGFR every 6–12 months and thyroid tests. Gentamicin (conventional every 8 h, US label): trough just before the next dose, avoid >2 µg/mL and prolonged peaks >12 µg/mL. High-dose methotrexate: urine pH ≥7 before infusion; serial levels from 24 h; leucovorin typically from 24–36 h until <0.05–0.1 µmol/L; HPLC after glucarpidase.
explanation.differs: Lithium (not protein bound, not metabolised, reabsorbed like sodium) vs gentamicin (trough reflects accumulation) vs methotrexate (urine pH and serial levels guide rescue); aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity (generally reversible) vs vestibular and auditory toxicity (generally irreversible); conventional dosing troughs (<2 µg/mL label) vs current once-daily AUC monitoring and <1 mg/L troughs.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the correct lithium sampling time; reading a lithium level against severity tiers and dialysis criteria; the next step for a high gentamicin trough; which aminoglycoside toxicity is irreversible; the urine pH needed before high-dose methotrexate; why methotrexate immunoassays mislead after glucarpidase.

questions.stem: A patient on long-term oral lithium needs a routine serum lithium level. When should the blood be drawn?

options.text: About 12 hours after the last dose
options.rationale: Correct. Routine lithium levels are drawn about 12 hours after the last dose, after the post-dose peak has passed.

options.text: About 2 hours after the last dose
options.rationale: Incorrect. Lithium peaks within hours of an oral dose, so a 2-hour level reads high and is not comparable with standard ranges.

options.text: Any time, because lithium is protein bound and levels are stable
options.rationale: Incorrect. Lithium is not protein bound, and its level changes with time after the dose.

options.text: Only after the patient develops symptoms
options.rationale: Incorrect. Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and needs regular monitoring, not only symptom-triggered levels.

questions.stem: A patient on conventional gentamicin every 8 hours has a trough of 3.4 µg/mL drawn just before the next dose. What does this most likely mean, and what is the best response?

options.text: The drug is accumulating; lengthen the dosing interval and check kidney function
options.rationale: Correct. The US label says to avoid troughs above 2 µg/mL; a high trough reflects accumulation, and lengthening the interval is one way to adjust.

options.text: The level is therapeutic; continue unchanged
options.rationale: Incorrect. A trough above 2 µg/mL on conventional dosing is too high and raises the risk of kidney and ear toxicity.

options.text: Increase the dose to improve bacterial killing
options.rationale: Incorrect. Raising the dose would worsen accumulation; the trough measures safety, not killing.

options.text: The kidney injury it predicts is always permanent, so stop all monitoring
options.rationale: Incorrect. Aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity is generally reversible; it is ear and balance damage that is generally permanent, and monitoring must continue.

questions.stem: Before a high-dose methotrexate infusion, a patient on bicarbonate-containing fluids has a urine pH of 5.8. What should happen?

options.text: Delay the infusion and adjust bicarbonate until the urine pH is at least 7
options.rationale: Correct. Methotrexate and its metabolites are poorly soluble in acidic urine; consensus advice is not to infuse until urine pH is at least 7.

options.text: Start the infusion; urine pH does not affect methotrexate
options.rationale: Incorrect. Acidic urine promotes methotrexate crystallisation in the tubules and acute kidney injury.

options.text: Acidify the urine further to speed excretion
options.rationale: Incorrect. Alkalinisation, not acidification, increases methotrexate solubility and excretion.

options.text: Give leucovorin before the infusion to replace alkalinisation
options.rationale: Incorrect. Leucovorin rescue starts after methotrexate (typically 24–36 hours); giving it too early can blunt the anticancer effect and does not prevent crystals.

claims.text: Lithium: sodium-like, not protein bound, not metabolised, excreted entirely in urine; ~80% of filtered lithium reabsorbed, mostly proximal tubule.
Lithium peaks within hours of an oral dose; routine levels drawn about 12 hours after the last dose.
EXTRIP steady-state guide: 1.5–2.5 mild, 2.5–3.5 moderate, >3.5 mEq/L severe, only a guide.

Extracorporeal treatment recommended if kidney function impaired and >4.0 mEq/L, or decreased consciousness, seizures or life-threatening dysrhythmias at any level; suggested >5.0; rebound after dialysis.
Long-term lithium: creatinine and eGFR every 6–12 months; thyroid tests before and during treatment.
Conventional gentamicin every 8 h: trough just before next dose, avoid >2 µg/mL (and prolonged peaks >12); high trough = accumulation; lengthen interval in kidney impairment.
Aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity generally reversible; vestibular and auditory toxicity generally irreversible; genetic susceptibility rare.
Current guidance: once-daily dosing with AUC monitoring in adults; trough <1 mg/L for multiple-daily synergy dosing.
Methotrexate >90% renal; poorly soluble in acidic urine and crystallises in tubules; hydration and bicarbonate to urine pH ≥7 before infusion.
Leucovorin typically from 24–36 h, dosed by serial levels from 24 h, until methotrexate <0.05–0.1 µmol/L; immunoassay interference by DAMPA after glucarpidase, HPLC preferred.
Reviewer: leucovorin rescue 18–36 h after high-dose methotrexate, continued until methotrexate <50 nM.
claims.note: Not taught as stated. Bielack 2024 gives a typical start of 24–36 h and Howard 2016 a target of <0.05–0.1 µM; protocols vary. An 18-hour start was not found in the sources read.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 24 Hit 13 grades lithium 1.5–2.5 slight–moderate, 2.5–3.5 severe and >3.5 mEq/L potentially lethal. The EXTRIP workgroup (Decker 2015) labels the same steady-state bands mild, moderate and severe, says they are only a guide, and bases dialysis on >4.0 mEq/L with impaired kidney function, >5.0 mEq/L, or decreased consciousness, seizures or dysrhythmias at any level; the lesson teaches the EXTRIP version (register flag rv-lithium-tiers-extrip).

Ch. 24 Hit 14 gives leucovorin rescue at 18–36 h until methotrexate <50 nM. The European consensus (Bielack 2024) gives a typical start of 24–36 h and Howard 2016 a target of <0.05–0.1 µM, with timing and dosing set by protocol; the lesson teaches the source ranges (register flag rv-mtx-leucovorin-window).

Ch. 24 Hit 16 gives a trough below 2 µg/mL for traditional thrice-daily gentamicin. This matches the US prescribing information for conventional dosing, but current guidance (Moore 2025) prefers once-daily dosing with AUC monitoring in adults and a trough below 1 mg/L for multiple-daily synergy dosing; the label is US-only and Philippine guidance is not covered (register flag rv-gentamicin-trough-current-practice).
